title: Hundreds of Election Deniers Will Be on the Ballot This November
gist: Data from nonpartisan nonprofit States United Action shows 197 election deniers on congressional and statewide ballots across 43 states for the November 3 midterms, including 33 seeking offices with direct election oversight on top of 27 already holding such posts in 20 states. The piece profiles five tracked races — Michigan Senate, Wisconsin and Ohio governor, and Nevada and Colorado secretary of state — and reports that 84 percent of Trump's election-related statements in Q2 2026 included an explicit fraud claim.

insights.claim: Following the primaries there will be 197 election deniers on the ballot for congressional and statewide races across 43 states in the November midterms, according to data from nonpartisan nonprofit States United Action.
insights.speaker: David Gilbert
insights.so_what: A specific, sourced count converts a diffuse narrative into a measurable political phenomenon spanning most states.
insights.quote: there will be 197 election deniers on the ballot for congressional and statewide races in the midterms across 43 states

insights.claim: The roster includes a sitting US congressman who voted against certifying the 2020 election results, a former state representative who integrated QAnon conspiracy theories into election denialism, and local election officials who have pushed baseless conspiracy theories about noncitizen voting.
insights.speaker: David Gilbert
insights.so_what: The mix spans federal, state and local tiers, meaning the movement is not concentrated at any single level of government.

insights.claim: There are already 27 election deniers across 20 states holding statewide offices with election oversight, such as secretary of state or attorney general, and 33 more will seek similar positions in November.
insights.speaker: David Gilbert
insights.so_what: Oversight offices set voting rules and prosecute alleged cheating, so control of them is the operative variable for 2028.
insights.quote: there are already 27 election deniers in 20 states who hold a statewide office with election oversight

insights.claim: The central concern of election experts is that deniers could obtain oversight of the 2028 presidential election process, corroding the system from within as the numbers of those in positions of public trust increase.
insights.speaker: David Gilbert
insights.so_what: The risk framing is institutional capture over multiple cycles rather than any single contested count.
insights.quote: This really is an attempt to corrode the system from within.

insights.claim: The movement is described as more powerful than ever and embedded at every level of government, pushing conspiracy theories from positions of real power.
insights.speaker: David Gilbert
insights.so_what: The nonprofit tracking the data frames this as escalation, not plateau, going into the cycle.
insights.quote: Election deniers are embedded at every level of government, pushing conspiracy theories from positions of real power.

insights.claim: Candidates have been emboldened by a groundswell of local groups and individuals working for years to promote baseless claims about mail-in voting, noncitizen voter fraud, and rigged voting machines.
insights.speaker: David Gilbert
insights.so_what: Grassroots infrastructure, not just top-down messaging, sustains the candidate pipeline.

insights.claim: Sixty percent of the president's statements referencing elections since the 2024 election included an explicit claim of fraud, rigging, or theft, according to States United Action data.
insights.speaker: David Gilbert
insights.so_what: Quantifying presidential rhetoric turns a qualitative impression into a trackable trend line.
insights.quote: 60 percent of Trump’s statements referencing elections since the 2024 election include an explicit claim of fraud, rigging, or theft

insights.claim: That share of fraud-referencing election statements rose to 84 percent in the second quarter of 2026.
insights.speaker: David Gilbert
insights.so_what: The sharp quarter-on-quarter escalation ahead of the midterms suggests intensifying rather than stable messaging.
insights.quote: That percentage has risen to 84 percent in the second quarter of 2026.

themes.theme: Tracked races and what winners could do

insights.claim: The Republican Senate nominee in Michigan, a former US representative, once called Trump's efforts to persuade Georgia's secretary of state to change results 'more gangster than presidential' and blamed him unequivocally for January 6, but now amplifies fraud claims about his own state.
insights.speaker: David Gilbert
insights.so_what: A documented reversal shows election denialism being adopted as campaign strategy rather than sincere belief.
insights.quote: Rogers appears to see election denialism as a winning campaign strategy.

insights.claim: Polls show the Michigan Senate race in a dead heat between the Republican nominee and Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed.
insights.speaker: David Gilbert
insights.so_what: Competitiveness means the denial-aligned strategy is not obviously costing votes.

insights.claim: The Republican candidate for Wisconsin governor signed onto a Texas lawsuit in December 2020 seeking to invalidate Biden's victory, voted against certifying Pennsylvania and Arizona results, suggested he would have overturned Wisconsin's too, and has welcomed an FBI investigation into the state's elections.
insights.speaker: David Gilbert
insights.so_what: The record is documented voting behavior, not just rhetoric, which is the strongest form of the evidence.

insights.claim: As Wisconsin governor, that candidate would have power to appoint some of the state's top election officials on the Wisconsin Elections Commission, enabling him to install election deniers to oversee voting for the 2028 presidential election, and initial polls show him slightly trailing Democrat David Crowley.
insights.speaker: David Gilbert
insights.so_what: Gubernatorial appointment power is an indirect but durable route to election administration control in a swing state.

insights.claim: The billionaire Republican candidate for Ohio governor has baselessly claimed the 2020 election was stolen by 'big tech' and called the January 6 attack an 'inside job' and 'entrapment,' providing no evidence for any of these claims.
insights.speaker: David Gilbert
insights.so_what: A self-funding candidate with national profile carries these claims into a major governorship race polling extremely tight.
insights.quote: Ramaswamy has also called the January 6 attack on the Capitol an “inside job” and “entrapment.”

insights.claim: That Ohio candidate supports voter-suppression measures enshrining restrictive voter ID law into the state constitution, and as governor would have much more power to force such measures through, deeply affecting the 2028 presidential election.
insights.speaker: David Gilbert
insights.so_what: Constitutional entrenchment of voter ID would be far harder to reverse than statutory change.

insights.claim: The Republican nominee for Nevada secretary of state calls being labeled an election denier a 'badge of honor' and helped arrange a QAnon coalition of candidates for the 2022 midterms, in which he lost to the incumbent he now faces again.
insights.speaker: David Gilbert
insights.so_what: A rerun of a race already lost tests whether denial-aligned candidacies have gained ground since 2022.
insights.quote: Former Nevada state representative Jim Marchant says being called an election denier is a “badge of honor.”

insights.claim: That Nevada candidate lacks establishment Republican support and filings from July show he had just $13.86 in his campaign war chest compared with over $1 million for his opponent.
insights.speaker: David Gilbert
insights.so_what: Extreme fundraising asymmetry suggests the denial brand does not automatically convert into donor support.
insights.quote: Filings from July show Marchant had just $13.86 in his campaign war chest, compared to over $1 million for his opponent.

insights.claim: His stated plans if elected include deregistering every single voter in the state, moving to paper ballots, and requiring all votes to be counted by hand, powers backed by a secretary of state's ability to change election procedures, advise county officials, and help certify statewide results for 2028.
insights.speaker: David Gilbert
insights.so_what: Mass deregistration plus hand counting would be the most disruptive administrative change any single state official could impose.

insights.claim: Colorado's Republican secretary of state candidate says his first act would be to delete the state's voter lists and force every citizen to reregister, which is illegal at both federal and state level, and he wants to eliminate all voting machines while placing all public records on the blockchain.
insights.speaker: David Gilbert
insights.so_what: A campaign platform built on an explicitly illegal first act signals willingness to test legal constraints from office.
insights.quote: his first act would be to delete Colorado’s voter lists and force every citizen to reregister. (This is illegal on both a federal and state level.)

insights.claim: That Colorado candidate has admitted using the ELLY tool to support his claim that up to 25 percent of registered Colorado voters have registration issues; ELLY was built by the creators of EagleAI, a tool made by a former doctor and used by conservative activists ahead of the 2024 election to challenge voter roll registrations, often based on inaccurate data.
insights.speaker: David Gilbert
insights.so_what: Private data-matching software is the technical engine converting bad data into mass voter challenges.
insights.quote: The ELLY tool was developed by the creators of EagleAI, a tool created by a former doctor which was used ahead of the 2024 election by conservative activists to challenge voter roll registrations

insights.claim: The Colorado Democratic opponent is the current Jefferson County clerk who previously ran a nonpartisan good-government advocacy group, and no public polling is available for either the Colorado or Nevada secretary of state races.
insights.speaker: David Gilbert
insights.so_what: Down-ballot administrative races carry outsized 2028 consequences yet attract no public polling attention.
